passages.t: Sheba's cry, and ten women set aside
passages.happening:
A worthless man named Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjamite, happens to be there. He blows the ram's horn and shouts, “We have no share in David, no inheritance in Jesse’s son. Every man to his tent, O Israel!” (verse 1). All the men of Israel desert David to follow Sheba. ‘But the men of Judah stayed by their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem’ (verse 2).

When David comes back to his palace in Jerusalem, he takes the ten concubines he had left to care for the palace and puts them in a house under guard. He provides for them, but he no longer sleeps with them. ‘They were confined until the day of their death, living as widows’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Absalom's revolt is over, but its wounds are open. At the end of chapter 19 the men of Israel and the men of Judah quarreled over who had more right to the king, and Judah's words were harsher. Sheba steps into that gap. He is from Benjamin, Saul's tribe, and resentment over the crown's passing from Saul's house comes up more than once in these chapters, as it did with Shimei.

The kingdom was still a loose union of tribes held together by the king himself, and the old line between the northern tribes, often simply called Israel, and Judah in the south ran deep. Sheba's cry shows how fragile the union still is. The word for worthless marks someone lawless and destructive. It is a judgment on a troublemaker.

The ten women had been left to keep the palace, and Absalom had taken them in public to claim his father's throne. David cannot go back to them, and he cannot send them away. So they live out their lives as widows in a guarded house, cared for and set aside. The text records it without comment, and the reader feels the cost of Absalom's act falling on women who had no say in any of it.
passages.later: The same cry was raised again, almost word for word, when the kingdom split under Solomon's son: “What portion do we have in David, and what inheritance in the son of Jesse? To your tents, O Israel!” (1 Kings 12:16).
passages.asks: Sheba turned an old grievance into a rebellion. Ask where you have seen resentment between groups used by someone who stood to gain from it. And ask who around you is bearing the cost of other people's choices, and what care for them would look like.

passages.happening:
David tells Amasa to call up the men of Judah within three days. Amasa takes longer than the time he was given. So David sends Abishai after Sheba before he can reach a fortified town, and Joab's men, the Cherethites and Pelethites and all the mighty men, march out (verses 4-7).

At the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa meets them. Joab is dressed for war with a dagger at his belt. “Are you well, my brother?” Joab asked Amasa (verse 9), and he takes Amasa by the beard with his right hand as if to kiss him. Amasa is not on guard against the dagger in Joab's hand. Joab stabs him, and Amasa dies on the road (verse 10). Then Joab and Abishai go on after Sheba.

One of Joab's young men stands by the body and calls out that whoever is for Joab and for David should follow Joab. But the troops stop where Amasa lies, so the man drags the body off the road into a field and covers it with a garment, and then all the men go on with Joab (verses 11-13).
passages.hearers:
David had promised Amasa, Absalom's former commander, the command of the army in place of Joab (19:13). It was meant to win back Absalom's supporters, and it humiliated Joab. Joab answers with a knife.

Taking a man by the beard to kiss him was an ordinary gesture of friendship, which is what makes the murder so treacherous. The chapter sets two meetings against each other. On the road a man meets a man with a greeting of peace and a hidden blade. At the wall of Abel, a woman will meet the same man with words, and a whole town will be spared.

The army stops to stare at the body in the road. Joab's man has to move it before they will follow. Even the soldiers know what they have seen.
passages.later:
A proverb names the kind of kiss Joab gave: ‘The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful’ (Proverbs 27:6).

On his deathbed David named this murder to Solomon, with Joab's killing of Abner, as blood that had to be answered: ‘He killed them in peacetime to avenge the blood of war’ (1 Kings 2:5).
passages.hard:
Why does Joab murder Amasa and face no consequence?

The text does not approve of Joab. It describes the killing in grim detail, and later David names Joab's murders of Abner and Amasa as crimes Solomon must answer. Joab goes unpunished in David's lifetime because David's hold on power depends on him, a weakness the story exposes and does not excuse. The consequences of David's earlier failures keep unfolding: the king who could not restrain the sons of Zeruiah at Hebron still cannot restrain them now.
passages.asks: Joab greeted Amasa as a brother and killed him in the same moment. Ask whether you have ever smiled at someone you meant to harm, in word if not in deed. And ask whom you are tolerating because you depend on them, when what they do is wrong.

passages.happening:
Sheba passes through the tribes to Abel-beth-maacah, and Joab's army besieges him there. They build a siege ramp against the outer wall, and the troops begin to batter it down.

Then a wise woman calls from the city, “Listen! Listen! Please tell Joab to come here so that I may speak with him” (verse 16). When Joab comes, she says, “Listen to the words of your servant” (verse 17). Long ago, she says, people went to Abel for counsel, and that is how disputes were settled. ‘I am among the peaceable and faithful in Israel, but you are trying to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why would you swallow up the LORD’s inheritance?’ (verse 19).

“Far be it!” Joab declared. “Far be it from me to swallow up or destroy!” (verse 20). He wants only one man, Sheba, who has lifted his hand against the king. The woman answers that Sheba's head will be thrown to him over the wall. She goes to the people with her wise counsel, they cut off Sheba's head and throw it to Joab, and Joab blows the ram's horn. The army goes home, and Joab returns to the king in Jerusalem (verses 21-22).
passages.hearers:
Abel-beth-maacah lay in the far north of Israel, near Dan and the headwaters of the Jordan, close to the border of the Aramean state of Maacah. Its name means something like meadow of the house of Maacah.

Siege warfare meant building a ramp of earth and stones against a city wall so that soldiers could bring battering equipment up to it. A siege could last weeks and end with the whole town destroyed.

The town's rescue comes through a figure Israel respected, a wise woman whose words carried weight, like the woman of Tekoa in chapter 14. She appeals to Abel's name as a place people went for counsel, to its standing as a mother in Israel, a leading town with villages around it, and to the land as the LORD's inheritance, which Joab would be swallowing up. The word for inheritance is the very word Sheba used when he said the north had none in David. A rebel used it to tear the people apart, and a wise woman uses it to plead for mercy.

The exchange at the wall is quick, with repeated calls to listen, and her question in verse 19 shames the general. The chapter sets her wisdom against Joab's dagger. Sheba's story opens with his horn and closes with Joab's.
passages.later:
Abel-beth-maacah would fall to foreign kings in later years, first to Ben-hadad of Aram (1 Kings 15:20) and then to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria, who ‘came and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah’ (2 Kings 15:29).

Deborah called herself by the woman's title for her town: ‘until I, Deborah, arose, a mother in Israel’ (Judges 5:7).
passages.hard:
Why does the wise woman hand over Sheba's head?

Her choice is hard. Sheba was a rebel under sentence for raising his hand against the king, and by the standards of that time his death was a legal penalty. She saved a whole town by giving up the one man the army wanted. Readers differ on how to weigh it. Some see a hard but just act of wisdom that saved many innocent lives. Others note that the story, like much of 2 Samuel, reports a violent world honestly without holding every act up as a model.
passages.asks: The wise woman saved her town with words, with knowledge of her people's history, and with courage. Ask what that kind of wisdom would look like in a conflict you are facing now. And ask whom you could call to listen before the wall comes down.

passages.happening: The chapter ends with a list. ‘Now Joab was over the whole army of Israel’ (verse 23). Benaiah is over the Cherethites and Pelethites; Adoram is in charge of the forced labor; Jehoshaphat is the recorder; Sheva is the scribe; Zadok and Abiathar are priests; and Ira the Jairite is David's priest (verses 23-26).
passages.hearers:
The list repeats, with changes, the one in 8:15-18, and the two lists frame the long account of David's family and Absalom's revolt in between.

The first name says much. Joab is back over the whole army. David tried to replace him with Amasa, and Joab answered with a knife. Now no one can move him, and David will warn Solomon about him on his deathbed.

One new office appears: Adoram, in charge of the forced labor. He seems to be the same man named Adoniram under Solomon and Adoram under Rehoboam, which suggests that the work gangs began under David, not only under Solomon.
passages.later: The same man appears under Solomon: ‘Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor’ (1 Kings 4:6). And under Rehoboam the north's anger fell on him: ‘King Rehoboam sent out Adoram, who was in charge of the forced labor, but all Israel stoned him to death’ (1 Kings 12:18).
passages.asks: The list ends the story of the revolt with Joab back in charge and a new office for forced labor. Ask what has been quietly settled in your own life after a crisis that should have been questioned. And ask who carries the heaviest loads in the order that has been restored.
